To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) Local adaptation to hosts was found for TEV.

(1) local adaptation was observed in a multihost experimental evolution of an RNA virus, (2) local adaptation was associated with host-specific mutations, and (3) a fitness trade-off for generalists was not observed in this experimental system.

(i) multihost pathogens can adapt to different hosts without a fitness cost; (ii) local adaptation is a widespread phenomenon among multihost plant pathogens, (iii) local adaptation is not necessarily accompanied by parallel evolution; (iv) local adaptation is associated with the accumulation of host-specific mutations; (v) the evolution of local adaptation is associated to a high degree of host specialization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of host-pathogen interactions in a context of experimental evolution.
the evolutionary dynamics of plant viruses in natural populations and their interaction with the environment.
the evolution of host specificity in a plant virus and the evolutionary mechanisms that maintain the genetic diversity in the host-pathogen interaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TEV genome is highly flexible and that it has a large capacity to adapt to new hosts.
local adaptation to a host is not costly in terms of performance, and that the cost of generalism is absent in our experimental conditions.
TEV can adapt to new hosts with no apparent cost in terms of fitness in other hosts, but that this adaptation does not necessarily involve parallel evolution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TEV is a generalist virus, with a high potential for adaptation to new hosts, and with a strong capacity to evolve in a multihost environment.
TEV is able to evolve rapidly and adapt locally in a multihost environment, but that the genetic basis of this local adaptation is not a simple one.
the evolution of TEV on different hosts was mostly driven by local adaptation, and that this process was not constrained by the existence of a generalist-specialist trade-off.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of plant viruses in natural hosts is more complex and dynamic than previously assumed.
local adaptation to hosts is a general phenomenon for multihost pathogens, which has important implications for the epidemiology of emerging diseases.
TEV can adapt to multiple hosts in the laboratory and, therefore, it is likely to be able to adapt to new hosts in nature.
